guide.title: Lower East Side, Manhattan: Tenements, Reform, and Reinvention
guide.intro: The Lower East Side was Lenape land before European settlement; its riverfront point, Corlears Hook, takes its name from Jacobus van Corlaer, a Dutch schoolmaster who settled there around 1638, and the wider area contained Dutch-era farms called 'bouwerij.' Some of the first tenements built in New York City went up at Corlears Hook in 1833, beginning the neighborhood's defining era of dense tenement housing. Waves of immigration followed: large German immigration in the 1840s created 'Kleindeutschland' (Little Germany), and by 1920 the neighborhood's Jewish quarter housed roughly 400,000 residents, with Yiddish theaters along Second Avenue. Tenement-reform movements, including Jacob Riis's work, culminated in First Houses (1935-1936) — the first public housing project in the United States. The Lower East Side Historic District was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2000, and amid rapid gentrification the National Trust for Historic Preservation placed the neighborhood on its 'America's Most Endangered Places' list in 2008.

sections.heading: An Immigrant Landmark, Restored
sections.body: The Eldridge Street Synagogue, built in 1887, survives today as the meticulously restored Museum at Eldridge Street — described as a symbol of immigrant aspirations realized, and listed by Time Out among the most beautiful buildings in the world. The Lower East Side Tenement Museum, founded in 1988 by Ruth J. Abram and Anita Jacobson, preserves an 1863 tenement at 97 Orchard Street and an 1888 building at 103 Orchard Street; it was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1994 and a National Historic Site in 1998.

sections.heading: Getting there by subway
sections.body: The heart of the Lower East Side is served by the Delancey St-Essex St station complex (F, J, M, Z), with the B/D at Grand St on the neighborhood's Chinatown border and the F at East Broadway covering the southern blocks — most visitors arrive via Delancey/Essex, one stop off the Williamsburg Bridge.

sections.heading: A Market and a Park for the Neighborhood
sections.body: Essex Market, billed as 'New York City's Most Historic Market,' has served the Lower East Side for over 85 years and now houses more than 30 vendors. A short walk away, Sara D. Roosevelt Park — opened in September 1934 and stretching seven blocks from Chrystie to Forsyth Streets — mixes basketball courts and a playground with community gardens like the M'finda Kalunga and Hua Mei Bird Gardens.

faq.question: How do I get to the Lower East Side by subway?
faq.answer: Take the F, J, M, or Z to Delancey St-Essex St, the neighborhood's main hub one stop off the Williamsburg Bridge. The B/D at Grand St and the F at East Broadway cover the northern and southern edges.

faq.question: What is the Tenement Museum?
faq.answer: Founded in 1988, it preserves an 1863 tenement at 97 Orchard Street and an 1888 building at 103 Orchard Street as a National Historic Landmark and National Historic Site, with restored period apartments open for public tours.

faq.question: How old is Katz's Delicatessen?
faq.answer: Katz's has been operating since 1888, making it New York City's oldest deli.

faq.question: Is the Museum at Eldridge Street open every day?
faq.answer: No — it's open Sunday through Friday, 10am to 5pm, and closed on Saturdays.

faq.question: Where can I stay on the Lower East Side?
faq.answer: The Ludlow Hotel (180 Ludlow St) and Hotel on Rivington (107 Rivington St) are both verified boutique hotels in the core of the neighborhood.

places.name: Sara D. Roosevelt Park
places.address: Chrystie St to Forsyth St, between E Houston St and Canal St, Manhattan
places.summary: Opened in September 1934 and named — over her own objection — for Sara Roosevelt, mother of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, the seven-block park includes basketball courts, soccer fields, a playground, and community gardens like the M'finda Kalunga and Hua Mei Bird Gardens.

places.name: Katz's Delicatessen
places.address: 205 East Houston Street (corner of Ludlow St), New York, NY 10002
places.summary: Operating since 1888, Katz's is New York City's oldest deli and the neighborhood's signature pastrami destination.

places.name: Russ & Daughters
places.address: 179 E. Houston St., New York, NY 10002
places.summary: An appetizing shop selling 'bagels & lox since 1914,' a fourth-generation family institution of the Jewish Lower East Side.

places.name: Yonah Schimmel Knish Bakery
places.address: 137 E. Houston Street, New York, NY 10002
places.summary: A knish bakery founded in 1910, one of the last old-world Jewish bakeries on Houston Street.

places.name: Clinton St. Baking Company
places.address: 4 Clinton Street (btw. East Houston & Stanton), New York, NY 10002
places.summary: A neighborhood restaurant famous for its pancakes (blueberry, banana walnut), celebrated annually with a 'Pancake Month.'

places.name: The Ludlow Hotel
places.address: 180 Ludlow St (between Houston and Stanton), New York, NY 10002
places.summary: A boutique hotel in the core of the Lower East Side, with on-site dining and drinking venues and event spaces.

places.name: Hotel on Rivington
places.summary: A glass-tower luxury hotel known for floor-to-ceiling glass walls, skyline views, balconies, and soaking tubs, with concierge services and neighborhood walking tours.
